title: Supplier Responses to Platform Recommendations in Business-to-Business Electronic Commerce
affiliations: University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business, Georgetown University, McDonough School of Business,  and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU)

detail.title: Supplier Responses to Platform Recommendations in Business-to-Business Electronic Commerce
detail.abstract: Business-to-business electronic commerce (B2B e-commerce) platforms increasingly use recommendations to connect suppliers with potential business opportunities in the form of buyers' requests for quotation (RFQs). Yet little is known about whether and how these platform recommendations affect supplier bidding behavior and bidding success. Using data from a constructionsector B2B e-commerce platform, we find that receiving a recommendation increases not only the probability of bidding on the recommended RFQs by 1.4 percentage points (direct effect) but also the probability of bidding on non-recommended RFQs by 0.7 percentage points (spillover effect). The positive spillover effect emerges because platform recommendations prompt suppliers to broaden their search and pursue additional opportunities beyond focal RFQs. However, the positive spillover effect does not translate into a higher probability of winning because spillover bids tend to target popular yet less relevant RFQs. Further, losing bids is positively associated with the likelihood of supplier churn over the subsequent six months. Collectively, we show that engagement-centric recommender systems in B2B markets may broaden supplier bidding participation without improving bidding success, highlighting the importance of accounting for trade-offs among multiple platform objectives.

title: Pricing a Participation-Dependent Product: Evidence from the Mega Millions Redesign
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD),  and New York University (NYU) - Department of Marketing

detail.title: Pricing a Participation-Dependent Product: Evidence from the Mega Millions Redesign
detail.abstract: We study pricing in a participation-dependent product: one whose value to each buyer depends on how many other buyers participate. The April 2025 Mega Millions redesign-a bundle that raised the base ticket price from $2 to $5 and changed the prize schedule-provides a rare opportunity to measure both channels. Using retailerlevel panels from New York and Texas and a national PDI point-of-sale panel, we find that Mega Millions revenue fell by 23-28%. In New York, where base-ticket quantity is observed cleanly, quantity fell by about two-thirds. We find little evidence of immediate substitution to Powerball, scratch tickets, or online gambling. Controlling for the advertised jackpot cuts the headline revenue decline roughly in half, consistent with a participation-feedback channel in which lower current sales slow jackpot growth and thereby depress future demand. We then calibrate the Compiani et al. (2025) expectedloss demand framework and simulate dynamic profit under the endogenous rollover process. Across three counterfactual pricing exercises, the participation-feedback-adjusted profit optimum lies below the implemented $5 price.

title: The Human Capital Allocation Framework: Optimizing Talent Allocation in AI-Driven Organizations

detail.title: The Human Capital Allocation Framework: Optimizing Talent Allocation in AI-Driven Organizations

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Human Capital Allocation Framework (HCAF) as a conceptual and empirical approach to how organizations allocate talent in an era of AI, skillbased staffing, and dynamic organizational design. The central proposition is that organizations suffer not only from talent shortages, but also from talent misalignment across assignments. HCAF reframes staffing decisions as a matching problem between talent characteristics, task requirements, and context. Using a PRISM-informed design, this study tests a bounded claim: whether more explicit, data-informed matching is associated with stronger assignment-level match quality and better downstream performance than traditional allocation under specified conditions. The study combines matched contrasts, case-based evidence, survey data, and organizational artefacts to evaluate when HCAF is useful, when its effects are conditional, and when the evidence is too weak to support stronger causal claims.

title: The Hallucination Problem And The Architecture Of Trust The Case for Legal-Specific Language Models in the Practice and on the Bench
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: The Hallucination Problem And The Architecture Of Trust The Case for Legal-Specific Language Models in the Practice and on the Bench
detail.abstract:
The legal profession's response to AI hallucination has converged on a verification model: lawyers must check what the machine produces before submitting it to a tribunal. This Article shows that the verification model rests on a premise three independent formal proofs falsify. Xu, Jain, and Kankanhalli establish through learning-theoretic diagonalization that any computable language model deployed as a general-purpose reasoner produces hallucinated outputs on at least some inputs. Kalai and Vempala derive from calibration theory a positive lower bound on the rate at which a calibrated model fabricates when queried about facts represented thinly in its training corpus. Simhi and colleagues empirically establish that prompt-level perturbations flip the same model from correct to confidently incorrect on a fixed factual question. The proofs operate in different mathematical frameworks and converge on the same conclusion: the lower bound on hallucination is positive, scale-invariant, and unaffected by improved prompting.

The Article advances three doctrinal claims. First, the impossibility results operationalize as a five-tier architectural spectrum running from general-purpose large language models through retrieval-augmented generation to deterministic retrieval and purpose-built Legal-Specific Language Models (LSLMs). The spectrum maps onto Factor 4 of the AI Legal Reference Model developed in a companion paper and supplies the architectural granularity that the venture-capital "copilot/autopilot" framing lacks. Second, the architectural distinction between stochastic generation and deterministic retrieval is doctrinally load-bearing: Model Rule 1.1, Model Rule 3.3, and ABA Formal Opinion 512 cannot be discharged by a lawyer who selects an architecture mathematically incapable of supplying the verification those rules require. Third, the profession's institutional response must specify a verified legal corpus, retrieval-first composition, and provenance-preserving outputs as load-bearing requirements of any AI system used in the practice of law.

Five-tier classification, doctrinal application across the early sanctions caseload (Mata, Park, Farris, Fletcher, Flycatcher), and the LSLM specification together establish that hallucination is not a verification problem to be managed but an architectural property to be designed against. Doctrine operates at the architectural level. The profession's regulatory response must answer at the same level.

title: Automation Adoption and Monopsony Power: Evidence from Chinese Firms
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics, United Nations and Central University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Automation Adoption and Monopsony Power: Evidence from Chinese Firms
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of automation technology diffusion on the monopsony power of Chinese firms. Drawing on the China Industrial Enterprise Database for the period 1998-2013 and supplementing it with industry-level robot data from the International Federation of Robotics (IFR), we reach three principal findings. First, the diffusion of automation technology significantly strengthens the monopsony power of Chinese industrial firms in labor markets. Second, mechanism analysis reveals that automation primarily operates through three channels: (i) substituting routine labor tasks and thereby weakening workers' outside employment options, which compresses labor supply elasticity; (ii) generating robot-labor complementarities that raise the marginal revenue product of labor while wages remain constrained by search frictions, widening the gap between marginal product and wages; and (iii) By displacing lower-wage routine workers and compressing the wage bill relative to output, robot adoption mechanically raises the share of fixed employment costs, further amplifying the markdown. Third, the effect exhibits a significant technology-efficiency threshold: firms with lower initial total factor productivity experience a more pronounced strengthening of labor market power following automation adoption, whereas high-TFP firms partially offset this effect through technological complementarity and human-robot collaboration. These findings reveal the adverse distributional consequences of industrial robot adoption for labor markets and provide microeconomic evidence to guide policymakers in curbing excessive concentration of labor market power while advancing intelligent manufacturing.

title: Two-Dimensional Gabor-Granger: A Pricing Research Method for Two-Attribute Tradeoffs

detail.title: Two-Dimensional Gabor-Granger: A Pricing Research Method for Two-Attribute Tradeoffs
detail.abstract:
Pricing research commonly uses the Gabor-Granger method for single-attribute price sensitivity or choice-based conjoint (CBC) for multi-attribute decisions. Many pricing problems sit between these two: healthcare patients weigh copay against wait time, fintech customers weigh interest rate against repayment term, telecom subscribers weigh price against data allowance, and streaming subscribers weigh price against ad load. While single-attribute methods ignore the second dimension, conjoint handles the tradeoff through a fitted utility model, which may be heavier machinery than the problem needs when only two quantitative attributes are in play. 

This paper describes two-dimensional Gabor-Granger (2D Gabor-Granger), a practitioner extension of the Gabor-Granger method for two-attribute pricing tradeoffs. Respondents complete a short adaptive sequence of choice or purchase-intent tasks over a grid of price and second-attribute combinations. Each answer classifies not only the tested combination but also the dominated region of the grid, producing respondent-level threshold points in the original attribute units, with no utility model, part-worths, or conversion step. The method can be deployed monadically or with one or more fixed competitive references. For 3×3, 4×4, and 5×5 grids, the maximum number of tasks needed to classify every tested combination as acceptable or unacceptable is 5, 8, and 10, respectively. 

A simulation modeled on healthcare pricing, using copay price and wait time for virtual versus in-person doctor visits, illustrates the standard pricing-research deliverables: a two-dimensional demand surface, iso-demand contours, revenue-maximizing prices at each level of the second attribute, and segment-level pricing outputs. The underlying adaptive-threshold mechanic is not new; the contribution is the packaging of that logic for commercial pricing research.

title: Day-to-Day Traffic Network Modeling under Route-Guidance Misinformation: Endogenous Trust and Resilience in CAV Environments
affiliations: and Purdue University

detail.title: Day-to-Day Traffic Network Modeling under Route-Guidance Misinformation: Endogenous Trust and Resilience in CAV Environments
detail.abstract: Connected and autonomous vehicles and smart mobility services increasingly use digital route guidance as an operational input to traffic network management. When this information becomes unreliable or adversarial, day-to-day traffic models must represent not only flow adaptation but also the evolution of user trust in the information source. This paper develops a coupled day-to-day traffic assignment and trust-evolution framework for route-guidance misinformation. Within-day congestion is represented by Lighthill-Whitham-Richards network loading, while day-to-day route choice follows bounded-rationality logit learning with trust-dependent reliance on external guidance. Trust is modeled as an aggregate class-level behavioral reliance state encoded by a Beta evidence model and updated from repeated guidance errors. Theoretical analysis establishes stationary equilibria, a conservative stability guide, a weighted compliance index for population-level vulnerability, and an asymmetric recovery law that explains post-attack trust hysteresis. Numerical experiments on Sioux Falls, with an Anaheim robustness check, show that endogenous trust creates a threshold-based resilience mechanism. Below the trust-activation threshold, the attack remains behaviorally stealthy and dynamic trust provides almost no attenuation. Above the threshold, trust erosion reduces the impact of the fixed-trust attack by about 91 percent in Sioux Falls and 85 percent in Anaheim. The experiments also show that CAV penetration increases fixed-trust vulnerability while preserving dynamic attenuation, and that traffic performance can recover before trust, resulting in a 77-day hidden vulnerability window. The results provide a trust-aware modeling basis for resilience analysis in CAV-enabled traffic networks.

title: Assessing the Impact of Online Shopping and Drone Delivery on Socio-Economic Profiles and CO2 Emissions
affiliations: Florida State University and Florida State University

detail.title: Assessing the Impact of Online Shopping and Drone Delivery on Socio-Economic Profiles and CO2 Emissions
detail.abstract: Online shopping and drone delivery has gained great popularity since COVID-19 pandemic. Given its potential for widespread deployment in cities to assist last-mile delivery, comprehensively evaluating its long-term effects on socioeconomic profiles and CO2 emissions is imperative. This paper proposes a novel urban economics model that quantifies these impacts within transportation networks. The model considers interactions between households, retailers, housing property developers, and the transportation system. Distinct from prior linear-city models, our framework explicitly incorporates network-wide congestion effects from commuters, shoppers, and delivery trucks. Numerical experiments conducted on the Sioux Falls network demonstrate that the introduction of online shopping reduces traffic congestion by 3% and annual CO2 emissions by 10%. Drone delivery captures a comparable market share to truck delivery and offers similar consumer delivery costs, and it proves more advantageous in reducing environmental impacts. This model is readily adaptable to other urban networks to assess the long-term implications of online shopping and drone delivery adoption.

title: Flawed Foundations: A Critical Assessment of the FTC's Proposed Multi-Level Marketing Earnings Claims Regulation
affiliations: Phoenix Center for Advanced Legal & Economic Public Policy Studies and Phoenix Center for Advanced Legal & Economic Public Policy Studies

detail.title: Flawed Foundations: A Critical Assessment of the FTC's Proposed Multi-Level Marketing Earnings Claims Regulation
detail.abstract: In response to the Supreme Court’s ruling in AMG Capital Management that the Federal Trade Commission lacks the legal authority to seek equitable monetary relief under Section 13(b) of the FTC Act, in January 2025 the Commission issued a series of rulemakings targeting earnings claims in multilevel marketing to streamline enforcement procedures. The Commission’s cost-benefit analysis estimates benefits ranging from $84 million to $1.09 billion over ten years, but we identify several elementary errors in its analysis that overstate benefits by an order of magnitude. Across a wide range of plausible parameter values in Monte Carlo Analysis, the proposed rule fails to pass the cost-benefit test. We also demonstrate that the Commission fundamentally misinterprets the evidence for their claim of widespread deception.

title: Mothers' Perceived Vulnerability, Perceived Threat, and Intention to Administer Preventive Medication to Their Children

detail.title: Mothers' Perceived Vulnerability, Perceived Threat, and Intention to Administer Preventive Medication to Their Children
detail.abstract: The present research addressed whether mothers' perception that their children are vulnerable to and threatened by a certain health problem increases their intention to use over-the-counter (OTC) medications to prevent it. The research aimed to examine the predictive validity and the moderating effects of perceived vulnerability and perceived threat on mothers' intention to administer over-the-counter preventive medications to their school-aged children. Derived from social cognition models, a causal model was developed and tested with data collected from 299 mothers in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, regarding the vitamin supplement category. The model was found to significantly predict mothers' intention to use OTC medications. Perceived vulnerability and perceived threat did not predict intention but moderated the relationship between perceived benefit and intention to administer vitamin supplements. Theoretical and managerial implications and limitations of the research are also discussed.

title: Invisible Until It Rains: Board Governance and Leadership Resilience in the Canadian Federal Public Service

detail.title: Invisible Until It Rains: Board Governance and Leadership Resilience in the Canadian Federal Public Service

detail.abstract: Board governance is associated with more durable employee perceptions of senior leadership when organizations face external stress, with no measurable gap in normal times. I test this claim using four cycles of Canada's Public Service Employee Survey, 2019 to 2024, covering thirteen federal organizations matched by mandate and workforce type. Before 2020, employees in board-governed organizations and in minister-direct departments rated senior leadership the same. After the COVID-19 pandemic struck, a four-point gap opened and held. The difference-indifferences estimate is 3.62 points (cluster-robust p = 0.031, wild cluster bootstrap p = 0.027), and the effect appears across all six senior management questions, with five of six surviving Benjamini-Hochberg correction at q = 0.10. The result is robust to leaveone-out resampling, an expanded eighteen-organization comparator group, an alternative dependent variable, a Schedule II only subsample, and a fourteen-organization stress-test that adds the Canada Energy Regulator (interaction = 4.02, bootstrap p = 0.014). The result attenuates to 1.32 under respondent-weighting (p = 0.31), which the paper discusses as a scope-of-claim question rather than a refutation. A within-organization case at the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, where the president's seat sat empty for fifteen months, points toward leadership stability as part of the underlying mechanism. The findings extend the corporate governance literature beyond agency-theoretic monitoring and toward the buffering function that emerges only under stress, and they identify three governance practices the mechanism implies are worth testing-succession depth, institutional memory, and engagement with the executive layer below the CEO.

title: Want Me to Conduct "Appropriate" Due Diligence? Ask "Reasonable" Things. How Vague terms shape behavior, Information Production and Governance in Sustainable Supply Chains
affiliations: Universidad Carlos III de Madrid

detail.title: Want Me to Conduct "Appropriate" Due Diligence? Ask "Reasonable" Things. How Vague terms shape behavior, Information Production and Governance in Sustainable Supply Chains

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Banking Institute Working Paper Series No. 208
publicationDetails.journalName: European Banking Institute (EBI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Due diligence laws, such as the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (2024/1760) which require companies to map, prevent, mitigate, and end adverse human rights and environmental impacts across their supply chains are controversial, as they are seen as a source of enforcement risk. Is that true? Current evidence suggests different. The expansion of liability for companies and groups, linked to developments in tort and company laws, seems unrelated to due diligence laws, which, for their part, seem to increase the information produced by companies and groups about their operations more than their liability risk. This article argues that this is a natural consequence of the use of terms such as “appropriate”, “reasonable”, “necessary” or “proportionate” to define due diligence duties. Such vague terms, and the way they are used, deter from strict enforcement, and promote information sharing. More broadly, vague terms influence (i) companies’ incentives, with potential deterrence, but also chilling effects, (ii) the evidentiary process, promoting discovery and accuracy over punishment, and (iii) corporate governance, creating a “comply or explain-plus” mechanism that promotes dialogue between companies, stakeholders and authorities. This enables the transmission of social norms and best practices… maybe. Under the right conditions. For that purpose, it needs to be used, and valued, by investors and consumers. In any event, acknowledging the role of vague terms and information production is essential to make a balanced assessment of due diligence laws.

reference: 46 Review of Litigation (forthcoming); SMU Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 737
title: New Corporate Geography: Reframing the Incorporation Decision
affiliations: Southern Methodist University - Dedman School of Law

detail.title: New Corporate Geography: Reframing the Incorporation Decision

publicationDetails.detailsText: SMU Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 737
publicationDetails.journalName: Southern Methodist University Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Corporate law conventionally treats the state of incorporation as the center of corporate governance. Under the internal affairs doctrine, fiduciary duties, shareholder rights, board authority, and internal corporate disputes are assigned to the charter state. That convention has long made Delaware the benchmark for sophistication, predictability, and governance quality, and it now frames debates over DExit, Texas reincorporations, and interstate charter competition. This Article challenges the premise that incorporation is the best proxy for where corporate governance occurs. 

The Article introduces "corporate geography" as a framework for evaluating incorporation and reincorporation decisions. Corporate geography asks where a firm is actually governed: where it operates, where it is regulated, where it litigates, where its subsidiaries are organized, where its contracts are performed, and where legal risk demands board and managerial attention. Drawing on Bloomberg Law company reports, litigation records, SEC filings, Form 10-K disclosures, Exhibit 21 subsidiary schedules, reincorporation proxy materials, and public-company governance documents, the Article examines ConocoPhillips and comparator firms across energy, telecommunications, healthcare distribution, digital assets, retail, real estate, consumer products, and technology. It proposes a three-part framework: firms should ask where governance actually occurs, what share of total governance risk is meaningfully shaped by internal-affairs doctrine, and whether Delaware's legal infrastructure provides marginal value sufficient to justify maintaining a separate legal domicile. 

The evidence shows that incorporation supplies an important but limited layer of governance. For many public companies, fiduciary litigation and internal-affairs disputes represent only a narrow portion of total legal exposure. Operational jurisdictions, regulatory regimes, commercial disputes, employment law, environmental law, consumer protection, securities regulation, intellectual-property litigation, public enforcement, subsidiary structures, and contractual obligations often do more continuous governance work. Even when fiduciary claims arise, the legally salient facts are frequently generated outside the charter state through regulatory investigations, enforcement actions, settlements, litigation, and operational failures. 

This reframing changes the stakes of reincorporation. Reincorporation does not necessarily relocate governance, nor does it necessarily signal an effort to evade accountability. It changes the formal legal regime governing a bounded set of internal affairs while leaving most operational, regulatory, contractual, and public-law constraints intact. Recent reincorporation disclosures are therefore better understood as claims about alignment, predictability, litigation management, statutory design, and operational fit than as conclusive evidence of managerial opportunism.


The Article does not argue that Texas, Nevada, or any other state is superior to Delaware, or that Delaware lacks value. It argues that Delaware’s value should be measured against the firm’s full governance denominator. Corporate law should reconsider the presumption that sophistication and predictability require Delaware incorporation when governance is produced primarily elsewhere. Governance follows operations, not incorporation.

title: Parameter Uncertainty and the Economic Returns to Cereal Breeding R&D
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Minnesota

detail.title: Parameter Uncertainty and the Economic Returns to Cereal Breeding R&D
detail.abstract: This study examines how uncertainty in two key parameters, research-induced cost savings (K-shift) and the timing of benefits (R&D lags), affects economic evaluations of cereal breeding research. Using a simulation-based approach calibrated with published studies, we assess the sensitivity of four common benefit-cost metrics: Net Present Value (NPV), Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR), Internal Rate of Return (IRR), and Modified Internal Rate of Return (MIRR). Results show that MIRR remains stable across uncertainty scenarios, while IRR, NPV, and BCR are highly sensitive to assumptions, particularly regarding the timing of benefit realization. Early adoption substantially increases IRR estimates, and variability in K-shift values generates wide dispersion in NPV and BCR results. When uncertainty in both parameters is considered jointly, these effects are amplified, increasing the risk of misestimation if parameters are not well calibrated. These findings support existing recommendations that favor MIRR as a more robust summary measure for agricultural R&D assessment. The paper also highlights limitations in current benchmarking practices, including reliance on historical and predominantly public-sector studies. By systematically analyzing parameter uncertainty, this study improves the rigor of benefit-cost analysis and offers practical guidance for analysts and policymakers involved in prioritizing agricultural R&D investments.

title: A Price Conscious Marketplace and Market Efficiency: An Analysis of Germany's Investigation into Marketplace Pricing Policies
affiliations: Auburn University - Department of Economics, Phoenix Center for Advanced Legal & Economic Public Policy Studies and Auburn University - Department of Economics

detail.title: A Price Conscious Marketplace and Market Efficiency: An Analysis of Germany's Investigation into Marketplace Pricing Policies
detail.abstract: On June 2, 2025, Germany's Federal Cartel Office (the Bundeskartellamt) issued a preliminary legal assessment alleging that Amazon's price-control mechanisms for marketplace sellers potentially violate both European and German competition law. On February 5, 2026, the agency issued (an outline of) a preliminary decision stating that Amazon must cease or adapt the behavior within nine months with specified requirements. One concern of the Bundeskartellamt regards Amazon's policy that third parties whose offers are "classified as 'significantly high prices' or 'uncompetitive prices' are excluded from appearing in the Buy Box; their display in the search results list is also restricted, and they may be excluded from advertising on Amazon." The Bundeskartellamt argues that Amazon's policy "restrict[s] the visibility of the sellers' offers and [] interfere[s] with their freedom to set their own prices." But does Amazon's policy, rooted in maintaining its reputation as a low-priced online marketplace, actually harm consumers? To answer this question, this BULLETIN develops a formal economic model to analyze the welfare implications of marketplace pricing policies in markets with heterogeneous consumers and demonstrates that a policy of excluding or downgrading excessively high prices directs purchases toward efficient firms and enhances economic welfare.

title: China's Mercantilist Squeeze on Developing Countries
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University and Peterson Institute for International Economics

detail.title: China's Mercantilist Squeeze on Developing Countries

publicationDetails.detailsText: Peterson Institute for International Economics Working Paper No. 26-7
publicationDetails.journalName: Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: China's resurgent trade surplus has revived concern in the United States and Europe, but consequences for low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) remain underappreciated. This paper documents a "China Squeeze": China's compression of the industrialization space poorer economies need in labor-intensive manufacturing. Using historical benchmarks and labor-endowment comparisons, we show that China, despite becoming richer and moving up the technology ladder, still commands a historically unusual share of global lowskilled manufacturing export markets. We estimate that this squeeze costs LMICs hundreds of billions of dollars in forgone exports. It also operates through rising Chinese import competition in LMIC markets and China's limited absorption of low-skilled imports from poorer countries. Macro evidence suggests that policy distortions, including exchange rate undervaluation, may have amplified the squeeze. The central concern is developmental: China's export strength may close off pathways to industrialization for poorer economies.

title: AI Exposure and Housing Markets
affiliations: University of Tulsa - Collins College of Business and Auburn University - Department of Finance

detail.title: AI Exposure and Housing Markets
detail.abstract: Generative AI arrived just as the pandemic had pushed housing demand away from expensive, supply constrained metros. We ask whether the period after Chat-GPT extended that dispersion or reversed it. Using a quarterly panel of 211 U.S. metros from 2017Q1 to 2025Q4, we relate Zillow and FHFA house price growth to AI Geography Exposure weighted by 2019 population, with the 2020 remote work break timed separately. AI exposed metros grow faster after 2023: a one standard deviation increase in AIGE is associated with 3.6% higher cumulative ZHVI growth, about $9,400 at the sample median 2023 home value. The premium also appears in FHFA prices and rents, concentrates in supply inelastic metros, and is reproduced by a predetermined LLM task suitability index. A pandemic WFH placebo has the opposite sign. IRS migration data show reduced outmigration from exposed metros, and Revelio LinkedIn data show rising AI hiring there. The early generative AI period appears to have reinforced the residential value of dense, supply constrained high skill labor markets, reversing the spatial direction of the pandemic.

title: MFF-TSA: A Multi-scale Feature Fusion Network for Track Segment Association
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: MFF-TSA: A Multi-scale Feature Fusion Network for Track Segment Association
detail.abstract: The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is widely relied on for maritime ship monitoring. The continuous track data provided by AIS is an important basis for real-time perception of ship dynamics and ensuring navigation safety. However, in practical applications, AIS signals are often disrupted by artificial shutdowns or environmental interference, which seriously affects the portrayal of the ship’s complete behavioural pattern and the investigation and judgement of abnormal situations. Most existing track segment association methods rely on predefined motion models and manually defined association rules, and suffer from poor model adaptability and limited feature discriminative ability in complex scenes. To address these problems, this paper proposes a Multi-scale Feature Fusion-based Track Segment Association algorithm (MFF-TSA). The method addresses the engineering challenge of correctly matching ship targets before and after AIS signal interruption, enabling reliable target re-identification under discontinuous observations. Through the parallel feature extraction module, the method deeply explores the implied local structure, global associations, and complex motion patterns among track segments at three levels: geometric distance, spatio-temporal context, and dynamic behaviour. Through the adaptive feature fusion mechanism, it effectively integrates the above multi-level and heterogeneous discriminative information, and achieves a more accurate association judgement in an end-to-end manner. Experiments on public and simulated datasets show that MFF-TSA achieves Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) values of 0.9681 and 0.9435, respectively, significantly outperforming existing mainstream methods. These results verify its comprehensive advantages in association accuracy and scenario adaptability, providing reliable technical support for continuous tracking and intelligent analysis of maritime targets’ behaviours.

detail.abstract: Since 2023, twenty-five states have enacted age verification laws requiring adult content websites to verify users’ identities. In response, major platforms like Pornhub have blocked access entirely in many states rather than implement verification systems. While the Supreme Court recently upheld the constitutionality of these laws in Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton (2025), this analysis questions whether these restrictions satisfy the constitutional requirement of being “substantially related” to protecting minors when measured against their actual costs and effectiveness.

title: Are Affiliated Pharmacies Paid More by PBMs? A Review of the Tennessee Audit
affiliations: Phoenix Center for Advanced Legal & Economic Public Policy Studies

detail.title: Are Affiliated Pharmacies Paid More by PBMs? A Review of the Tennessee Audit
detail.abstract: The Tennessee audit, which has been cited in recent Senate hearings as evidence that PBMs systematically favor their affiliated pharmacies with higher reimbursement rates, found that Express Scripts paid its affiliate pharmacies more than non-affiliates for 568 of 2,318 medications studied (24%). This analysis reveals that the auditor used an incorrect statistical baseline and failed to employ proper methodology for detecting systematic discrimination. Under proper statistical analysis, finding that affiliated pharmacies received higher reimbursements in only 24% of cases actually provides strong evidence that Express Scripts was favoring unaffiliated pharmacies, not its affiliates.

title: Updating EPFD Limits: An Economic Analysis
affiliations: Auburn University, Phoenix Center for Advanced Legal & Economic Public Policy Studies and Auburn University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Updating EPFD Limits: An Economic Analysis
detail.abstract: This BULLETIN examines the economic rationale for modernizing 25-year-old equivalent power flux density (EPFD) limits governing satellite spectrum sharing. Using an economic model of differentiated competition, we show that increased consumer demand for non-geostationary (NGSO) broadband services-which did not exist when current standards were established-calls for more permissive interference standards. NGSO services are growing at 27% annually and projected to overtake traditional geostationary revenues by 2028, yet face regulations designed for a pre-NGSO market. Our analysis demonstrates that cost reductions for expanding NGSO services outweigh penalties for declining networks, supporting the FCC's approach of optimizing interference tolerance for consumer welfare rather than treating it as an absolute constraint.

title: Maturity Alignment Matters: The Predictive Power of the Variance Risk Premium
affiliations: Masaryk University - Department of finance and Masaryk University

detail.title: Maturity Alignment Matters: The Predictive Power of the Variance Risk Premium
detail.abstract: The predictive power of the variance risk premium (VRP) for realized volatility depends critically on aligning option maturity with the forecast horizon. Historically, short-dated index options were restricted to the monthly cycle, forcing interpolation between distant expirations and contaminating the VRP signal with horizon-irrelevant variance. The CBOE's staggered introduction of Friday (2010), Wednesday (2016), Monday (2018), and Tuesday/Thursday (2022) SPY weekly expirations generates a sequence of regimes with varying alignment feasibility. Using SPY options from October 2013 to December 2025, we decompose the VRP into a Friday-only component and an alignment differential capturing the signal from non-Friday expirations. Within a nested HAR framework, the Friday-aligned VRP delivers large out-of-sample gains under MSPE, QLIKE, and realized utility. The alignment differential adds significant improvements at the one- and five-day horizons in later regimes, with the clearest effect at the one-day horizon in the post-2022 daily-expiry regime. Gains attenuate with forecast horizon.

title: Flexible Labor Contracts, Firm-specific Pay, and Wages
affiliations: Williams College, Tilburg University and Tilburg University

detail.title: Flexible Labor Contracts, Firm-specific Pay, and Wages
detail.abstract: We use matched employer–employee administrative data for the Netherlands to study the labor market effects of flexible employment contracts. Using an Abowd– Kramarz–Margolis (AKM) framework, we show that flexible contracts are associated with lower wages, a greater volatility of worked hours, and a higher probability of unemployment in the following year. However, our findings indicate that the disadvantages associated with flexible contracts arise not only from the contractual arrangement itself, but also from the types of firms in which flexible workers are employed. Specifically, workers on flexible contracts are disproportionately employed at lower-paying firms with lower firm-specific wage premiums. Furthermore, we find that flexible workers benefit less from employment at more profitable, larger, and financially safer firms, and that local labor market concentration amplifies their wage disadvantage. Overall, our findings imply that the negative effect of flexible contracts on wages may be overstated if the types of firms at which flexible workers are employed are not taken into account.

title: Information Pollution and the AI Information Trap: Revisiting Grossman-Stiglitz in the Age of Algorithmic Monocultures
affiliations: Willamette University - Atkinson Graduate School of Management

detail.title: Information Pollution and the AI Information Trap: Revisiting Grossman-Stiglitz in the Age of Algorithmic Monocultures
detail.abstract: We extend Grossman-Stiglitz with Free AI traders who observe a costless signal contaminated by a common hallucination but cannot detect the contamination. Free AI endogenously eliminates the uninformed class. The model nests Grossman-Stiglitz as a special case and yields a sharp result: above a threshold hallucination variance, AI adopters are objectively worse off than a hypothetical rational uninformed deviator in the same equilibrium, though they perceive adoption as beneficial. Three mechanisms sustain this information trap: unrecognized contamination, misoptimized demand, and impaired self-correction. At higher variance, a numerical phase transition turns freeriding into over-adoption. We characterize the optimal corrective tax.

title: Trajectory Optimization in Single and Dual-UAV Bearing-Only Target Localization
affiliations: National University of Defense Technology, National University of Defense Technology, National University of Defense Technology and National University of Defense Technology

detail.title: Trajectory Optimization in Single and Dual-UAV Bearing-Only Target Localization
detail.abstract: Bearing-only target localization is a fundamental problem in optical measurement and finds extensive applications in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) technology. Effective trajectory planning establishes favorable observation geometries, thereby enhancing the target localization accuracy of bearing-only UAV systems. This paper proposes an trajectory optimization method for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in bearing-only target localization scenarios. By leveraging the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), the proposed approach dynamically integrates the geometric configuration and vehicle maneuverability into the optimization framework. Specifically, we introduce a spectrally-weighted FIM objective function that provides better gradient dynamics near degenerate configurations, enabling the planner to rapidly escape from poor observation conditions. For dual-UAV scenarios, an intersection angle sine term is introduced to optimize triangulation geometry by improving the sight-line intersection angle, thereby preventing trajectory aggregation. Furthermore, we propose an improved Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithm with motion model constraints and particle normalization to ensure the physical feasibility of the trajectory and enhance the compatibility with the objective functions. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method reduces the median localization error by 99.21% compared to conventional FIM-based approaches in single-UAV scenarios, and achieves a 69.70% improvement for dual-UAV configurations, exhibits superior performance in long-duration bearing-only target localization of maneuverability targets at extended ranges.

title: The French Deep Tech Entrepreneurial Ecosystem: State of the Art and Future Challenges
affiliations: École Nationale Supérieure des Mines de Paris - Centre de Gestion Scientifique (CGS)

detail.title: The French Deep Tech Entrepreneurial Ecosystem: State of the Art and Future Challenges
detail.abstract: Deep tech has become a strategic priority for governments, investors, and industry actors seeking to address major societal and geopolitical challenges, including climate change, energy transition, health resilience, digital security, and technological sovereignty. This article examines deep tech not as a sectoral label, but as an entrepreneurial innovation regime characterized by research-based ventures, long development cycles, high uncertainty, capital intensity, and strong dependence on ecosystem complements such as specialized infrastructures, regulatory pathways, industrial partners, standards, and lead customers. Drawing on the French case, the article analyzes how deep tech has been progressively institutionalized as a core pillar of national innovation and industrial strategy, particularly since the late 2010s. France has developed significant upstream capabilities through research excellence, talent pipelines, public R&D support, technology transfer structures, and early-stage de-risking mechanisms. These efforts have positioned the country among Europe's most active deep tech ecosystems, with visible strengths in domains such as artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, space, climate and energy technologies, robotics, advanced materials, and TechBio/biotech. However, the analysis also highlights a structural imbalance between upstream asset generation and downstream conversion. While France performs strongly in the creation and early support of deep tech ventures, persistent bottlenecks remain in growth-stage financing, access to pilot and industrialization infrastructures, market entry, regulatory predictability, procurement, and lead-market formation. The article argues that moving from deep tech emergence to deep tech dominance requires strengthening deployment capacity and the connective tissue linking research, markets, and industrialization. This entails scaling patient capital and growth finance, expanding demonstration and industrial infrastructures, simplifying contracting and intellectual property processes, and accelerating market formation through procurement, standards, and early reference customers.

title: Cognitive Models for Market Price Formation
affiliations: , University of Perugia and University of Bologna Department of Statistics

detail.title: Cognitive Models for Market Price Formation

declarations.funderStatement: The second author acknowledges the support of the AIDMIX and RATIONALISTS research projects of the University of Perugia, funded under the FRB-2021 and FRB-2022 programs.

detail.abstract: We introduce a simple agent-based market price model firmly grounded in the principles of quantitative neurosciences and mathematical psychology. Once market orders are recognized as decision-making processes like any other, they can effectively be treated through the established paradigms in the field of the mathematical modeling of cognition. In this respect, we assume buy and sell orders to follow one of the best-known cognitive models of decision in a binary selection scenario, the Ratcliff (1978) diffusion decision-making (DDM) model, based on a double barrier Brownian hitting problem. By incorporating price and return feedback in the DDM order flow, and arranging the investors' trading attitude in a Zipfian ranking, we are able to satisfactorily reproduce a good number of market stylized facts. This neuroeconomics price formation paradigm supports the view that market structure fundamentally remains a reflection of human cognition, and the ways it shapes decision-making.

title: The Effects of Recent Federal Immigration Enforcement on California's Private Sector Employment
affiliations: University of California at Merced, , University of California at Merced and University of California at Merced

detail.title: The Effects of Recent Federal Immigration Enforcement on California's Private Sector Employment
detail.abstract:
The UC Merced Community and Labor Center analyzed Current Population Survey data for the periods before and following escalations in federal immigration enforcement actions in California. The center examined changes in the number of workers in California and the rest of the US, for the weeks of May 11, June 8 and July 6, 2025, and found that persons reporting private sector work in California decreased by 4.9%-with citizens forming a greater share of the decrease. The state's downturn in work is comparable with the Great Recession and the COVID-19 pandemic, and has profound implications for policymaking. 
KEY FINDINGS Findings indicate federal immigration enforcement actions have had a disruptive effect on California's economy. Fewer Californians reported private sector work during the week of escalated enforcement actions on June 8 than on the preceding reference week of May 11, 2025-and even fewer reported work the week of July 6. The May-July decline was greater for citizens (414,832) than noncitizens (327,659), though rates of decline were highest among noncitizens. In contrast, in the rest of the US, the number of citizen workers slightly increased while noncitizen workers remained almost the same.

title: The Effects of Medicare on Access to Preventive Care and Medication: Evidence from a Regression Discontinuity Design
affiliations: University of Toronto, University of Toronto and

detail.title: The Effects of Medicare on Access to Preventive Care and Medication: Evidence from a Regression Discontinuity Design
detail.abstract: Existing literature on the effects of Medicare on health outcomes focuses largely on pre-COVID-19 data with limited understanding of demographic stratification. This paper seeks to revisit the question of Medicare efficacy on health outcomes for various disadvantaged groups in the United States with a focus on outcomes before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Using National Health Interview Survey data sourced from the Integrated Public Use Microdata Series, we implement a fuzzy regression discontinuity design at age 65 and find that Medicare coverage has a statistically significant positive effect on insurance coverage and self-reported health status but insignificant effects on utilisation of preventive care and medication. These effects vary among different subgroups in the United States, with consistently larger coverage gains going to disadvantaged groups, whereas the effect on health outcomes for these groups is mixed. We also observe an attenuation of Medicare's effects on coverage during the peak and immediate aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as differences in its effects on health outcomes across different years.

title: T+1 Settlement and Market Quality: Evidence from India's Phased Rollout
affiliations: and Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda (MS)

detail.title: T+1 Settlement and Market Quality: Evidence from India's Phased Rollout

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available secondary market data and does not involve human participants. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper estimates the causal effect of accelerated equity settlement on market quality using India's phased transition from T+2 to T+1 settlement on the National Stock Exchange as a natural experiment. The rollout proceeded in 27 weekly batches from February 2022 to January 2023, sequenced by ascending market capitalisation, providing staggered treatment timing across 2,056 stocks. We estimate two-way fixed effects regressions and three heterogeneity-robust estimators-Callaway-Sant'Anna (2021), Sun-Abraham (2021), and a Goodman-Bacon (2021) decomposition-on 898,181 stock-day observations from January 2021 to March 2023. Our primary results are: first, T+1 settlement significantly reduces Parkinson volatility by 3.6% relative to its mean (β =-0.000034, p = 0.004), a finding that is consistent across all specifications; second, treatment effects on liquidity are heterogeneous-large-cap stocks experience significant illiquidity reductions (β =-0.000669, p = 0.005), while mid-cap stocks face adjustment costs (β = 0.006928, p < 0.001), both findings robust to size-specific time trend controls; third, the Goodman-Bacon decomposition confirms no negative TWFE weights, and the divergence between CS and Sun-Abraham ATTs reflects differential cohort weighting rather than estimation error. These results carry direct policy relevance for regulators in the United States, European Union, and other markets currently implementing T+1 mandates.

title: Productive Legitimacy: The Structural Layer That Makes Deliberative Systems Politically Consequential

detail.title: Productive Legitimacy: The Structural Layer That Makes Deliberative Systems Politically Consequential

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares a conflict of interest as Founder and President of the Paris School of Entrepreneurship (PSE), discussed in this paper; all conclusions are drawn from publicly verifiable sources. No external funding was received. No original dataset is presented; quantitative references draw exclusively from publicly available OECD publications cited in the reference list. AI-assisted writing tools (Claude, Anthropic) were used in a research assistant capacity — supporting structural organisation, literature identification, and language refinement under the author's direction; all intellectual positions, the productive legitimacy framework, the research direction, and the institutional evidence base are the author's own, and full responsibility for the content is accepted.

detail.abstract: University deliberative assemblies are working as designed-and that may be precisely the problem. This paper argues that procedural sophistication, however refined, cannot substitute for the structural condition that makes deliberation politically consequential: productive legitimacy. The claim is not that assembly design is inadequate. It is that design operates downstream of a precondition it cannot itself supply-and that until that precondition is named and built, the gap between deliberative ambition and institutional response will persist regardless of how well participants deliberate. The proliferation of deliberative assemblies documented and facilitated by the UNIDELIB network since 2020 provides the empirical landscape against which this argument is developed-it is precisely because the network has successfully institutionalised these spaces that the question of what would make them politically transformative becomes urgent rather than hypothetical. The paper engages Habermas's communicative rationality tradition not to refute it but to identify its missing foundation. The ideal speech situation assumes speaker standing as given. University deliberative assemblies assume it as procedurally conferred by the act of institutional invitation. Both assumptions do the same work: they bracket the question of why decision-makers should treat assembly outputs as binding rather than advisory. The legitimacy chain proposed here runs accordingly-agency derives from influence; influence from substantiation; substantiation from demonstrated contribution, intellectual and economic. Drawing on institutional economics and the theory of credible commitment (Williamson, 1985; North, 1990), the paper develops productive legitimacy as the structural layer that deliberative systems theory (Parkinson & Mansbridge, 2012) has not yet named. The structural constraints are taken seriously. French university governance exhibits a characteristic high power-distance pathology: legitimate deliberation architecturally isolated from consequential decisions, shaped by national centralisation, the grandes écoles hierarchy, and ministerial authority over institutional autonomy. OECD comparative data on higher education governance autonomy place French universities consistently below the OECD average across organisational, financial, and academic dimensions (OECD, 2023). A Nordic contrast case-the Danish tradition of medbestemmelse and the institutionalised co-determination structures of universities such as Aarhus and Copenhagen-demonstrates that lower power-distance governance architectures produce deliberative bodies with materially greater binding force. The framework predicts both failure and success cases. The paper further identifies a structural parallel between two contemporary legitimacy failures: the breakdown of credential-based signaling in the labor market (Autor, 2014; OECD, 2024) and the stagnation of procedural inclusion in university governance. Both are symptoms of proxy-based legitimacy failure (Akerlof, 1970; Spence, 1973). Both point toward the same institutional response: move from proxy to proof, from credential to contribution, from granted voice to earned standing. The paper closes by proposing a hybrid institutional design model integrating production-based legitimacy pathways into existing French governance structures-conseils d'administration, conseils académiques, and the deliberative assemblies the UNIDELIB network has institutionalised-with explicit equity architecture ensuring that access to productive standing is structured into the curriculum rather than captured by the already-advantaged. Crucially, deliberative assemblies are not merely precursors to political change-they are evidence of it. This paper's argument is not that assemblies have failed, but that they have succeeded well enough to deserve more: the productive infrastructure that would substantiate their participants' contributions, deepen their influence, and extend their transformative reach toward the durable institutional change that UNIDELIB's mission demands.

title: Emergency Financing and Macroeconomic Recovery after Large Natural Disasters
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Emergency Financing and Macroeconomic Recovery after Large Natural Disasters
detail.abstract: Large natural disasters create sharp macroeconomic pressures by damaging productive capacity, weakening fiscal revenues, raising reconstruction needs, and generating external financing gaps. This paper studies whether rapid emergency financing can support recovery after such shocks. We examine standalone IMF post-disaster financing through ENDA, the RCF, and the RFI using a synthetic control approach. Disaster episodes receiving IMF support are compared with similar untreated episodes matched on pre-disaster growth, disaster severity, and country characteristics. The results suggest that IMF-supported episodes recover faster than synthetic counterfactuals, with output gains lasting up to three years. These gains are accompanied by higher government spending, larger grant inflows, stronger imports, and a more front-loaded increase in public debt. The findings are consistent with emergency financing relaxing liquidity constraints, supporting countercyclical fiscal policy, and catalyzing external support, while highlighting the need for credible medium-term fiscal frameworks after recovery.

title: Transfer-Induced Debt Dynamics in Sovereign Default

detail.title: Transfer-Induced Debt Dynamics in Sovereign Default
detail.abstract: During the 2010s, the Greek sovereign debt crisis necessitated unprecedented EU financial aid accompanied by austerity conditions. Despite reforms to government spending and taxation, limited consolidation of social transfers led to unexpected expansions in transfer payments. This paper constructs a strategic sovereign default model, calibrated to Greek data, to examine the effects of transfer shocks on sovereign debt spreads. Under high financial stress (e.g., the elevated spreads at the onset of the 2010 Economic Adjustment Program), positive transfer shocks exacerbate already excessive absorption and significantly raise spreads. Under milder stress, these shocks initially produce negligible increases in spreads but lead to persistently higher spreads over the longer term. Stricter transfer-side austerity can mitigate crises and may avert default.

title: From Willingness to Action: The Willingness-Behavior Gap and Targeted Policies for Rural Energy Transition in Resource-Dependent Regions
affiliations: Taiyuan Normal University, Guangzhou University, Chongqing Technology and Business University and Taiyuan Normal University

detail.title: From Willingness to Action: The Willingness-Behavior Gap and Targeted Policies for Rural Energy Transition in Resource-Dependent Regions
detail.abstract: The energy transition in resource-dependent regions is crucial for achieving global sustainable development(SDG 7). However, this process is hindered by a persistent gap between transition willingness and actual behavior among rural households. Based on an analytical framework of willingness-behavior dynamics and employing data from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) complemented by field research in Shanxi Province, this study investigates the structural causes of this gap and its underlying mechanisms. The empirical analysis reveals three main findings: (1) A systematic binary opposition exists between the mechanisms driving behavior and willingness. Transition behavior is primarily constrained by rigid systems, such as village energy infrastructure and household economic capital, while willingness is driven by flexible signals, including market incentives and environmental awareness. (2) Social capital exerts a double-edged sword effect: micro-level networks create a social lock-in that inhibits transition, whereas community-level norms generate a positive peer effect that promotes it. (3) An effectiveness hierarchy exists within the flexible signal system, where direct economic incentives outperform macro policy signals, and the effect of environmental values becomes more pronounced after controlling for outliers. Based on these findings, this study proposes a targeted policy paradigm: for the unwilling group, policy should focus on activating flexible signals via market incentives; for the willing but inactive group, the key is to overcome rigid constraints through infrastructure and financial tools. This research provides theoretical insights and policy recommendations for addressing the last-mile challenge in the energy transition of resource-based regions.

title: A general and efficient time-domain random fatigue analysis method under non-stationary non-Gaussian random excitations
affiliations: Chongqing University, Chongqing University, Chongqing University, Chongqing University and Chongqing University

detail.title: A general and efficient time-domain random fatigue analysis method under non-stationary non-Gaussian random excitations
detail.abstract: Fatigue damage assessment under complex non-stationary non-Gaussian (NS-NG) random loadings remains a challenging problem in structural engineering, as existing time- and frequency-domain fatigue analysis methods suffer from inherent limitations in accuracy and applicability. This study develops a generalized, high-efficiency time-domain random fatigue analysis method for structures under NS-NG excitations. The Johnson transformation model and a sample-interpolation-based technique are introduced to realize accurate and fast generation of NS-NG random excitations. Inspired by the explicit time-domain method (ETDM), an explicit time-domain expression of hotspot stress for linear multi-degree-of-freedom structures is derived, and an efficient equation-solving strategy is proposed to conveniently determine the unknown coefficient matrices. Based on the obtained stress responses, structural fatigue damage is evaluated using the rainflow counting algorithm and cumulative damage criteria, and the statistical characteristics of fatigue damage can be determined by the Monte Carlo simulation. Numerical comparisons with different time- and frequency-domain methods demonstrate that the proposed method provides an accurate, efficient and broadly applicable solution for fatigue analysis under complex random loadings.

title: Accurate assessment of the failure probability of a concrete gravity dam based on near-fault ground motion parameter inversion
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Accurate assessment of the failure probability of a concrete gravity dam based on near-fault ground motion parameter inversion
detail.abstract: The Xiaqu concrete gravity dam is located only 5 km from the nearest segment of the Jiali fault zone. The assessment of its seismic failure probability under near-fault conditions depends heavily on the accuracy of the input ground motion. Based on historical seismic records from the dam area, this study fitted empirical relationships among the pulse period (Tp), peak ground velocity (PGV), moment magnitude (Mw), and epicentral distance (R). Considering the randomness of ground motion parameters including Mw, R, peak ground acceleration (PGA), and PGV, a near-fault ground motion generation method based on high- and low-frequency superposition was established. Utilizing this method and a combined oblique incidence mode of P- and SV-waves, 1,000 finite element seismic response analyses were conducted. Furthermore, a nonlinear mapping between ground motion parameters, oblique incidence angles, and dam displacement responses was established using an intelligent algorithm. By using the results of a specific finite element analysis as monitoring data, the Mw, R, PGA, PGV, and combined oblique incidence angles of the earthquake were determined through inversion. Random ground motions were then generated while preserving the inherent stochasticity of the seismic waves. Finally, the failure probability of the dam under this specific earthquake was accurately assessed using a comprehensive damage index. This was achieved through a variable weight efficacy coefficient method that integrates multiple indices, including the overall damage index, relative displacement at the dam crest, and cumulative sliding at the dam foundation and sliding blocks.

title: Ethics of Automation and Artificial Intelligence in Health Care Delivery
affiliations: University of Florida - Department of Medicine, University of Oklahoma - College of Medicine, Medical College of Wisconsin, Federation of State Medical Boards and Johns Hopkins University - School of Medicine

detail.title: Ethics of Automation and Artificial Intelligence in Health Care Delivery

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Dr. D'Souza has nothing to declare. Mr. Spear has nothing to declare. Dr. Ehrenfeld reports prior service on the American Medical Association Board of Trustees. Dr. Chaudhry reports serving as the CEO of the Federation of State Medical Boards. Dr. Miller reports prior service as a Medical Officer at the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
