detail.abstract: 1. ABSTRACT Background Diaspora engagement in Africa in health sectors of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) is often confined to financial remittances or short-term missions, failing to harness the potential for long-term health systems strengthening (HSS). We examined the transformative potential of diaspora-led institutions through a 25-year case study of People to People (P2P) in Ethiopia. Methods We used a combination of methods to study this case over a long period of time, from 1999 to 2026. Our methodology was informed by Yin's guidelines for longitudinal case studies. We collected our information by looking at old records, talking to 18 people involved in the project, including the founders, government officials, and those who benefited from it, and by looking at numbers such as the number of people trained, the number of hours volunteers spent, and the worth of the resources. Findings P2P started back in 1999 to help with HIV/AIDS, and over time it's grown into a strong system for improving healthcare. Some of the big things it's done include teaching over 100 specialists in areas where they're really needed, like emergency medicine, cancer treatment, and brain health. It's also set up 10 special programs for specific types of medicine. P2P helped Ethiopian medical schools get recognized internationally and brought in $45 million in donations and resources. By 2026, P2P has started AI integration into health systems program with Tibebe - Ghion Hospital - Bahir Dar university to assist around 100,000 patients annually. The secret to making all this work in the future was a special partnership between people of the Ethiopian community who lived abroad and local organizations in the West. Interpretation This case study suggests that diaspora institutions can engage in long-term, sustainable capacity building and mitigate health worker shortages in resource constrained settings like Ethiopia.

title: VIREM: A Variational Intelligence–Risk–Energy ManagementFramework for Decision-Centric and Explainable Smart Energy Systems
affiliations: Alfaisal University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Université de Moncton

detail.title: VIREM: A Variational Intelligence–Risk–Energy ManagementFramework for Decision-Centric and Explainable Smart Energy Systems
detail.abstract: Modern smart energy systems operate under increasing uncertainty, renewable intermittency, nonlinear demandvariability, and distributed operational constraints. Although recent artificial intelligence approaches have achievedstrong in-domain predictive performance, many remain primarily prediction-centric and therefore limited in uncertaintyhandling, operational interpretability, decision stability, and adaptive risk-aware control. To address these limitations,this work introduces VIREM, a Variational Intelligence–Risk–Energy Management framework designed for intelligentand explainable decision-centric energy-system analysis.The proposed framework is grounded in the Unified Variational Intelligence Framework (UVIF), which interpretsintelligent behavior as an adaptive variational process balancing prediction quality, uncertainty, operational risk, controlcomplexity, information gain, and decision stability. Within this formulation, energy-management decisions aremodeled through an information-driven optimization process integrating forecasting, cross-domain shift analysis, latentoperational-regime modeling, uncertainty-aware reasoning, and explainable decision analysis within a unified mathematicalframework.Experimental evaluations on internal renewable-energy data and an external UniSolar transfer dataset show thatVIREM achieves strong in-domain forecasting while revealing severe cross-domain degradation under shifted environmentalconditions. Rather than masking this degradation, the framework exposes it through elevated uncertainty, largervariational objective values, altered latent-regime distributions, and changed stability patterns. These results demonstratethe value of VIREM as a diagnostic and decision-support framework for interpreting operational mismatch, uncertaintygrowth, and regime instability in renewable-energy systems.Overall, VIREM advances a perspective in which AI evolves from a pure prediction engine toward an adaptive,uncertainty-aware, and operationally interpretable decision-support system for smart energy management.

title: How does monetary policy affect corporate innovation along the supply chain? The role of suppliers'  financial multiplier
affiliations: Nankai University, Nankai University, Nankai University and Nankai University

detail.title: How does monetary policy affect corporate innovation along the supply chain? The role of suppliers'  financial multiplier
detail.abstract: This study presents granular evidence that highly leveraged suppliers magnify the propagation of contractionary monetary policy shocks through supply chains. Drawing on Chinese supply-chain data covering 2015Q1–2024Q1, we find that monetary tightening triggers sharper declines in innovation among downstream customers tied to high-leverage suppliers than among those linked to low-leverage suppliers. Mechanism analysis reveals that, when suppliers are highly leveraged, tightening monetary conditions disrupt supplier–customer relationships and dampen knowledge diffusion along the supply chain, thereby eroding downstream innovation. Moreover, this amplification is especially pronounced when suppliers provide more relationship-specific inputs and when customers face higher switching costs.

title: The role of local authorities in health risk governance in Senegal: a One Health perspective
affiliations: University of Liège, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The role of local authorities in health risk governance in Senegal: a One Health perspective
detail.abstract: What is already known about this topic?One Health governance has predominantly relied on national intersectoral platforms operating through functional, often crisis-driven logics. In sub-Saharan Africa, decentralization reforms have formally transferred a range of health-related responsibilities to local governments. However, these actors remain largely absent from the design and implementation of One Health frameworks. Senegal illustrates this dual dynamic particularly well: while it has been a pioneer in institutionalizing One Health at the national level, it also features one of the most advanced decentralized governance systems in West Africa. This coexistence reveals a persistent disconnect between nationally coordinated One Health mechanisms and territorially grounded public action.What this report adds?Through a cross-sectoral analysis of human, animal, environmental, and plant health governance in Senegal, this study shows that local authorities are structurally marginalized within One Health frameworks, not by deliberate exclusion but by institutional design. The national One Health mechanisms follow a multi-level, intersectoral, and functionally driven logic, yet they lack formal links to the territorial jurisdictions of communes and departments. In practice, local authorities already handle key health-related functions, waste management, livestock markets, urban planning, and public hygiene, all of which directly affect health risks. However, these local actions remain poorly valued within official One Health structures, preventing coherent coordination between national and local governance.What are the implications for public health practice?In countries with decentralized governance architectures, local authorities represent a strategic level for overcoming the sectoral fragmentation inherent to One Health and embedding its preventive dimension within local territories. Three conditions are identified as necessary: formal recognition of local authorities' role in regulatory frameworks, dedicated resource transfers, and functional inter-level coordination mechanisms. The ongoing development of Senegal's second National Action Plan of Health security (NAPHS) provides a concrete policy window to advance this governance reform and offers a replicable model for other West African countries pursuing integrated, territory-based One Health governance.

title: MD-GNN: A Multimodal Graph Neural Network Framework for Comprehensive Drug–Drug Interaction Prediction
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Beijing Institute of Technology and The University of Hong Kong

detail.title: MD-GNN: A Multimodal Graph Neural Network Framework for Comprehensive Drug–Drug Interaction Prediction
detail.abstract: Accurate prediction of drug–drug interactions (DDIs) is vital for clinical safety. Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel at modeling DDI graphs, existing methods often underutilize heterogeneous drug information and fail to integrate graph structural priors into multimodal modeling. Specifically, performing cross-modal alignment independently of interaction topology limits biological consistency.​ We propose MD-GNN, a structure-guided multimodal framework that jointly models chemical structures (SMILES), pharmacological text, and mechanism pathways. MD-GNN employs modality-specific encoders to capture complementary biochemical and semantic features. To facilitate fine-grained reasoning, we introduce a cross-drug cross-attention mechanism that aligns modality pairs across drugs. Crucially, the DDI adjacency matrix is incorporated as a structural bias within the attention computation, guiding representation learning toward biologically plausible interactions. Furthermore, an adjacency-adaptive gating mechanism dynamically modulates modality contributions based on graph context to produce interaction-aware fused representations. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that MD-GNN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in multi-class and multi-label settings. Robustness analyses under label and feature perturbations further confirm its stability and generalization. These results highlight the importance of integrating multimodal drug features with structure-aware modeling for achieving reliable, interpretable, and biologically meaningful DDI prediction.

title: When Shorts Go Public: Mandatory Short Position Disclosure and Management Guidance
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management, University of Texas at Dallas, University of Texas at Dallas and

detail.title: When Shorts Go Public: Mandatory Short Position Disclosure and Management Guidance
detail.abstract: We examine whether mandatory public disclosure of large short positions and the short sellers' identities affects corporate voluntary disclosure decisions by exploiting the 2012 EU236 Rule, which requires public disclosure of short positions exceeding 0.5% of share capital. We find that EU firms increase both the propensity and frequency of management guidance issuances after the regulation. This effect is more pronounced for small firms, firms with low analyst coverage, and firms in countries with greater exposure to short selling threats and stronger regulatory enforcement. Further analyses reveal that the post-regulation guidance is of higher quality (more quantitative, broader, and detailed), has more negative tone, and elicits stronger and more negative market reactions. Finally, EU firms that increase guidance experience a subsequent reduction in large short positions, consistent with voluntary corporate disclosure deterring short selling pressure. Collectively, our findings suggest that the salience of the public disclosure of large short positions and the short sellers' identities motivates firms to increase voluntary disclosure.

title: Sectoral Heterogeneity in Monetary Policy Transmission:,Evidence from New Zealand’s Concentrated Banking System

detail.title: Sectoral Heterogeneity in Monetary Policy Transmission:,Evidence from New Zealand’s Concentrated Banking System
detail.abstract: This study examines sectoral heterogeneity in monetary policy transmission within a concentrated banking system, with implications for financial stability and macroprudential policy design. Analysing New Zealand’s five major banks during the 2020–2025 monetary policy cycle, we document large differences in interest rate sensitivity between mortgage and agricultural lending, exceeding the bank-size heterogeneity reported in foundational credit channel literature. Mortgage lending exhibits an Official Cash Rate (OCR) coefficient of +9,847 (NZ$ million per percentage point), while agricultural lending shows near-zero sensitivity (-197), with small and medium enterprise (SME) lending occupying an intermediate position (+1,536); we caution that the positive coefficients for mortgage and SME lending reflect substantial endogeneity and should be interpreted as conditional associations rather than causal elasticities. Cross-bank correlation analysis reveals near-perfect synchronisation in mortgage lending (r = 0.987) contrasting with minimal coordination in agricultural credit (r = 0.115), indicating that standardised products transmit policy uniformly while relationship-intensive sectors permit strategic differentiation. We argue that growth velocity is a more informative transmission metric than lending levels during supply-constrained periods. Growth rate deceleration ranged from 59% to 88% across sectors. The findings extend the credit channel framework of Kashyap and Stein (2000) to the sectoral dimension and support continued development of sector-specific macroprudential tools alongside aggregate monetary instruments in concentrated banking systems.

title: Optimal Imperfect Collusion: Price Randomization and Favor Exchange in Cartels
affiliations: Yonsei University and University of Rochester - Simon Business School

detail.title: Optimal Imperfect Collusion: Price Randomization and Favor Exchange in Cartels
detail.abstract: We analyze the sustainability of collusion in infinitely repeated symmetric first-price procurement auctions with complete information. We show that strategies combining on-path price randomization and continuation payoff rewards for losers enable collusion in this canonical model for a wider range of discount factors than previously recognized. Our theory can explain imperfect collusive bid rotation schemes as well as observed cartel behavior in which seemingly deliberate deviations from collusive pricing happen and are followed by internal reallocations of future business rather than cartel breakdown.

title: Science À La Mode? Institutions and Agenda Setting in Brain Research
affiliations: Université de Montréal, Universidad Nacional de Cordoba, Université de Montréal, University of Montreal and University of Montreal

detail.title: Science À La Mode? Institutions and Agenda Setting in Brain Research
detail.abstract: This study examines how research agendas in neuroscience have evolved over time. Drawing on a large-scale bibliometric and topic modeling analysis of 3 million scientific publications and 20 thousand patents, we show that agenda-setting neuroscience is dependent on both authors’ institutional affiliation and the possibility of commercialization of research through patenting. Using data from the Web of Science and USPTO databases, we identify 495 research topics and map their evolution over time by relating topic prevalence and publications’ impact with the type of affiliated and funding institutions, namely universities, governments, firms, hospitals, and nonprofits. Overall, results show a clear division of labor: universities publish, governments fund, and firms patent. However, this structure is shifting over time: we observe a transition from basic research on brain mechanisms toward applied, technology-driven, and patentable domains, particularly in neurodegenerative diseases and neurotechnologies. Furthermore, universities are increasingly patenting, while firms produce fewer but more influential publications. These findings suggest that specific institutional incentives have oriented neuroscience toward commercially viable areas, raising questions about the research priorities and the balance between innovation, public health, and fundamental knowledge production.

title: The Double-Edged Sword of Guanxi: Informal Transaction costs, Credit Access, and Rent Extraction in Chinese SME Lending
affiliations: University of Nottingham, Ningbo - University of Nottingham Ningbo China, University of Nottingham Ningbo China, University of Nottingham, Ningbo - University of Nottingham Ningbo China and Cardiff University Business School

detail.title: The Double-Edged Sword of Guanxi: Informal Transaction costs, Credit Access, and Rent Extraction in Chinese SME Lending
detail.abstract: Using survey data on 678 Chinese SMEs, this paper reframes gifts, hospitality, and entertainment (GHE) spending, a key manifestation of guanxi, as informal transaction costs incurred to navigate institutional voids in the credit market. We find that higher GHE spending is associated with greater loan access, larger loan amounts, and longer maturities, yet simultaneously with higher interest rates, stricter guarantee requirements, and lower borrower satisfaction. These patterns are robust to endogeneity corrections using instrumental variables and a conditional mixed process framework, as well as to Heckman selection correction for voluntary GHE disclosure. The results reconcile two seemingly opposing perspectives: GHE facilitates soft information transmission, relaxing credit constraints, while its asset specificity creates lockin, enabling lender holdup and rent extraction. This dualmechanism framework advances relationship banking theory by showing that informal transaction costs can expand the credit frontier while systematically extracting borrower surplus, highlighting a central tension in emerging market finance.

title: The Bidirectional Gate: A Novel Architecture for Machine-Verifiable Legal Constraint Enforcement

detail.title: The Bidirectional Gate: A Novel Architecture for Machine-Verifiable Legal Constraint Enforcement
detail.abstract: All prior smart contract systems and algorithmic decision systems share a common architectural limitation: they implement one-directional constraint evaluation. Inputs enter the system unchecked; outputs are filtered after generation. This paper introduces the Bidirectional Gate-a novel architectural mechanism that implements two independent axiomatic evaluation pipelines: an Ingress Gate, which evaluates every input against a formal constraint set before it enters system state, and an Egress Gate, which evaluates every output against the same constraint set before it is transmitted or committed. The Bidirectional Gate is the central architectural innovation of the Normative Smart Contract (NSC), deployed on Polygon Mainnet on April 4, 2026 (US Patent Pending 19/383,582). This paper provides the first complete theoretical treatment of the Bidirectional Gate: its formal definition, its logical properties, its legal significance as a mechanism for converting soft legal constraints into hard architectural constraints, and its application across five consumer-protection verticals. The paper proves that the Bidirectional Gate eliminates a specific category of harm-Ingress Contamination Harm-that output-only filtering cannot address, establishes the Bidirectional Gate Theorem (that the only compliant system state is one in which both gates pass), and situates this contribution within the computational law, smart contract, and algorithmic fairness literatures.

title: Optimal Investment and Pension Policy in Pay-as-You-Go Systems Under Forward Utility and Ageing Population
affiliations: Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB) - Department of Mathematics, CREST-ENSAE, Université Sorbonne Paris Nord and Université Sorbonne Paris Nord

detail.title: Optimal Investment and Pension Policy in Pay-as-You-Go Systems Under Forward Utility and Ageing Population

keywords: Mixed PAYG Pension with Buffer Fund Schemes

detail.abstract: This paper investigates optimal investment and pension policies in a Pay-As-You-Go (PAYG) system supplemented by a buffer fund used as an intergenerational risk-sharing mechanism. The social planner's preference criterion is represented by non-zero volatility forward Constant Relative Risk Aversion (CRRA) utilities, and explicitly accounts for both sustainability and adequacy constraints. The optimal policies are characterized in closed form, and an in-depth analysis of the impact of preference sensitivities on the pension scheme is conducted. A detailed numerical analysis is performed to evaluate the sustainability and benefit adequacy of this hybrid PAYG-buffer-fund arrangement under a range of demographic, financial, and macroeconomic scenarios.

title: SLATE: Shapley-LIME Attribution for Trajectory Explanations of Generative Models

detail.title: SLATE: Shapley-LIME Attribution for Trajectory Explanations of Generative Models
detail.abstract: SHAP and LIME are the two dominant model-agnostic explainability methods for tabular and classification settings, but neither extends gracefully to generative models. SHAP's coalitional foundation requires a meaningful notion of feature absence, which token masking does not provide for natural language; its computational cost is also prohibitive at the granularity at which generative models operate. LIME's local surrogate is more flexible, but it is unstable, kernel-dependent, and offers no theoretical guarantees. We introduce SLATE (Shapley-LIME Attribution for Trajectory Explanations), a unified framework that combines the cooperative-game foundation of SHAP with the local-surrogate fidelity of LIME, adapted to the structural realities of autoregressive generation. SLATE makes four contributions. First, it operates over semantic chunks of both input and output, producing an attribution matrix rather than a vector and enabling sentence-and claim-level explanations rather than token-level noise. Second, it replaces masking with counterfactual semantic substitution drawn from a calibrated reference distribution, keeping perturbations on the language manifold. Third, it fits weighted least squares surrogates with a hybrid Shapley-LIME kernel that recovers Shapley values asymptotically while retaining LIME's local-fidelity guarantees in finite samples. Fourth, it introduces trajectory regularisation, a temporal smoothness penalty that exploits the sequential structure of generated outputs and reduces estimation variance unconditionally and improves mean squared error when adjacent output segments share attribution structure (a smoothness condition stated explicitly in §5.4). We sketch convergence, fidelity, and sample-complexity results, describe an algorithm with computational complexity comparable to KernelSHAP, and outline an empirical validation programme spanning synthetic ground truth, hallucination detection, and human-alignment studies. Applications to regulated lending, model risk management under PRA SS1/23, and AI-generated content detection are discussed.

title: Employee Retirement Allocations as Involuntary Disclosure of Information about Firm Performance
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics (SUFE) - Dishui Lake Advanced Finance Institute (DAFI) and

detail.title: Employee Retirement Allocations as Involuntary Disclosure of Information about Firm Performance
detail.abstract: We examine whether mandatory disclosure of participant-directed defined-contribution plans reveals value-relevant information embedded in employees' retirement allocations. Using comprehensive Form 5500 data from 2003 to 2023, we study changes in employees' holdings of employer stock in DC plans and test whether these aggregated allocation decisions contain information about contemporaneous firm performance not fully reflected in analyst expectations. We find that increases in employee ownership predict positive earnings surprises. We further show that this information is incorporated into prices in two stages: first around earnings announcements and then around Form 11-K disclosures that reveal aggregated plan holdings to investors. The relation is stronger when external information frictions are high and disappears in sponsor-directed plans. Overall, the evidence identifies this disclosure as an important involuntary disclosure channel through which aggregated employee information enters earnings expectations and stock prices.

title: Doing Good, Investing Less? Substitution Effects between Digital Climate Engagement and Green Investment
affiliations: University of Toulouse 1 - Toulouse School of Economics (TSE), University of Bergamo - Department of Management, Economics and Quantitative Methods,  and Renmin University of China - School of Economics

detail.title: Doing Good, Investing Less? Substitution Effects between Digital Climate Engagement and Green Investment
detail.abstract: We study whether daily environmental actions substitute for or complement green investment. Using microdata from a digital platform that combines carbon-tracking features with mutual fund investing, we link users' carbon-reducing actions to their portfolio choices. Consistent with a model of individuals deriving decreasing marginal utility from their overall environmental impact, we find that green-point collection is negatively associated with green investing, and a promotion that increases the effectiveness of digital climate engagement crowds out green investment. Platform initiatives that raise environmental awareness instead spur green investment. Our findings reveal the nuanced impact of digital climate engagement on household financial decisions.

title: How the Central Emergency Response Fund Crowds in Bilateral Humanitarian Aid
affiliations: Stockholm University

detail.title: How the Central Emergency Response Fund Crowds in Bilateral Humanitarian Aid
detail.abstract: The United Nations Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) is central to peacebuilding and disaster relief, yet we know little about its capacity to fulfil one of its core functions, mobilizing donor countries to give bilateral aid in the event of rapid onset and underfunded humanitarian emergencies. This article argues that the aid given bilaterally by individual donor countries follows the choices made by the CERF to provide humanitarian aid, as bilateral donors seek enhanced aid coordination and delivery. The argument yields two hypotheses, which are examined by using a dataset for aid flows from the CERF, 29 Development Assistance Committee (DAC) donors, and 147 aid recipients between 2006 and 2021. The main findings are twofold. First, they suggest that bilateral humanitarian aid follows CERF aid. Second, the crowding-in effect of CERF aid does not appear to depend on donor country size. These results are robust even when addressing endogeneity, controlling for several other multilateral aid flows, and including various fixed effects. The article concludes by discussing broader implications for the literatures about aid catalyzation, aid coordination through IOs, and the determinants of humanitarian aid flows more broadly. doi:10.1093/isagsq/ksag082

title: A Gendered Activity Account: Construction, Measurement and Capital Investment Implications in Australia
affiliations: Government of the Commonwealth of Australia, Swinburne University of Technology - Department of Accounting, Economics, and Finance and Government of the Commonwealth of Australia - Department of Health

detail.title: A Gendered Activity Account: Construction, Measurement and Capital Investment Implications in Australia
detail.abstract: We constructed a novel gender-based thematic account for Australia that disaggregates Gross Value Added (GVA) across more than 500 ANZSIC industry classes by gender from 1994-95 to 2023-24 using an output-associated income method, corresponding to the 2025 System of National Accounts framework. The resulting female GVA share (W_F) captures both female employment share and relative female pay within each industry. Merging this measure with administrative data from the ABS Business Longitudinal Analysis Data Environment (BLADE), we found a robust negative relationship between W_F and capital intensity measured by capital expenditure to labour cost ratio (CapEx/Wages) across 9,897 industryclass-year observations. The effect is concentrated in market-based industries and absent in government-administered sectors. Finally, exploiting Australia's Workplace Gender Equality Act 2012 as a transparency shock, we found that the Act shifted W_F upward but did not independently affect capital intensity; the negative slope attenuated by approximately 55 per cent post-Act, providing empirical evidence that the Act addresses informational barriers, by creating accountability pressures on employers. However, structural undervaluation of feminized work still persists.

title: Pandemic-Induced Dynamics of U.S. Travel Behavior: Evidence from Three National Surveys and Implications for Pooled Rideshare Recovery
affiliations: Clemson University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Government of the United States of America - Argonne National Laboratory, Government of the United States of America - Argonne National Laboratory, Government of the United States of America - Argonne National Laboratory, Ford Motor Company and Clemson University

detail.title: Pandemic-Induced Dynamics of U.S. Travel Behavior: Evidence from Three National Surveys and Implications for Pooled Rideshare Recovery
detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic significantly reshaped individuals' travel behaviors, especially reducing the use of pooled rideshare due to health and safety concerns. This study investigates the impacts of the pandemic on pooled rideshare adoption and broader travel mode choice shifts using three national survey studies conducted in 2021, 2022, and 2025. Through latent class analysis, we identify five consistent user segments: ’Never Used/Never Will’, ’Shared Modes Dropouts’, ’Shared Modes Reducers’, ’No Change’, and ’All Modes Increasers’. These segments reflect diverse pandemic-related travel behavior change. Weighted demographic comparisons, mixed logit modeling, and ordinal logistic regression were further performed to reveal segment-level differences in sociodemographic composition, trip attribute sensitivities, and preferences for pooled rideshare experience optimization. Over time, a dominant trend of increasing reliance on private vehicles emerged, but signs of gradual recovery in shared mobility use were observed. Results suggest that user groups like ’Never Used/Never Will’ and ’Shared Modes Dropouts’ are more representative of lower-resourced transit users, and demonstrate low openness to future pooled rideshare experience optimizations. The ’No Change’ group is representative of mid-aged middle-class transit users with travel habit inertia-driven resiliency to the pandemic, who also show low openness to future pooled rideshare optimizations. The ’All Modes Increasers’ and ’Shared Modes Reducers’ groups are more representative of younger, wealthier, and urban-residing transit users, marking the highest potential for re-engagement in pooled rideshares. By tailoring interventions to the motivations and barriers of each segment, this study contributes to designing resilient, user-centered pooled rideshare services in the post-pandemic era.

title: Divergence in Climate Change Communication: LLM-based Evidence from the IPCC and the Press
affiliations: Department of Economics,  and University of San Andres (UdeSA)

detail.title: Divergence in Climate Change Communication: LLM-based Evidence from the IPCC and the Press

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: Nothing to declare

detail.abstract: Public summaries of IPCC climate assessments lean toward the more severe end of the technical evidence. The pattern appears at two stages: the IPCC's lead authors and member governments produce the Summary for Policymakers (SPM) from the Technical Summary (TS), and newspapers then cover the SPM. We use LLMs to score about 115,000 matched claim pairs from all six Assessment Reports (1990 to 2023) and ten major US and UK outlets. Both stages systematically shift toward the more severe end of the source while staying inside the IPCC's accepted scientific ranges. The shift comes mainly from emphasizing higher-impact magnitudes within reported ranges, less from uncertainty compression, and almost none from selecting worst-case emissions scenarios. Left-and right-leaning outlets show similar patterns.

title: Common Ownership and the COVID-19 Investment Shock
affiliations: Bradley University - Foster College of Business

detail.title: Common Ownership and the COVID-19 Investment Shock
detail.abstract: Common ownership has been argued to attenuate the sensitivity of corporate investment to firm-level Tobin's Q through governance-internalization across portfolio firms. The 2020 COVID-19 shock generated unusually large dispersion in firm-level Q while temporarily disrupting normal competitive optimization, providing a setting in which to assess whether the attenuation channel is contingent on the underlying firm decision problem. Using the Backus-Conlon-Sinkinson 13F holdings panel for 2013-Q3 through 2021-Q4, I document a three-phase pattern: the κ_sole-mediated Q-investment attenuation is -0.0050 (t = -2.79) in pre-COVID quarters, statistically indistinguishable from zero during the acute COVID shock (β = +0.0007, t = 0.07), and -0.0141 (t = -2.20) in 2021. The pattern is difficult to reconcile with mechanical accounts of common-ownership effects and is consistent with a state-contingent governance channel.

title: Sectoral Impacts of El Niño and Climate Change on India's Industrial Economy: A Case Study on Sustainable Economic Resilience
affiliations: , Independent Researcher and Tongmyong University

detail.title: Sectoral Impacts of El Niño and Climate Change on India's Industrial Economy: A Case Study on Sustainable Economic Resilience

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: ## Ethics Approval Statement The study was conducted in accordance with institutional research guidelines and ethical standards. All participants involved in the study participated voluntarily, and informed consent was obtained wherever applicable. No sensitive personal data were disclosed in the research. ### Ethics Approval Ethical approval was not required for this study as it involved secondary data analysis and non-invasive academic research methods.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this study.

detail.abstract: Purpose - This study examines the implications of El Niño on the Indian industrial economy in the context of climate change, with a focus on sectoral risks, economic disruptions, and emerging growth opportunities. Design/Methodology/Approach - The study adopts a qualitative and analytical approach using historical El Niño trends, secondary economic data, sectoral performance analysis, and climate-related industrial indicators to evaluate the impact on major industries in India. . Findings - The findings indicate that El Niño negatively affects agriculture, commodity supply chains, and food inflation due to weak monsoon conditions and rising temperatures. However, industries related to cooling appliances, irrigation and water technologies, renewable energy backup systems, healthcare, and consumer durables show strong growth potential during El Niño years. Climate change is further accelerating the demand for climate-resilient infrastructure and adaptive industrial strategies. Originality/Value - This study provides an integrated perspective linking climate phenomena with industrial economics in India. It highlights how El Niño acts not only as an environmental risk but also as a catalyst for industrial transformation, investment opportunities, and climate-resilient economic development

title: From Trade to Tax: Financial Development as a Mediating Channel in Developing Countries
affiliations: and

detail.title: From Trade to Tax: Financial Development as a Mediating Channel in Developing Countries

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funding.

detail.abstract: Domestic revenue mobilisation remains a critical challenge for developing economies, yet the interplay between trade openness, financial development, and tax revenue has not been subjected to formal mediation analysis. This paper tests the hypothesis that financial development mediates the relationship between trade openness and tax revenue in a panel of 90 developing countries over the period 2000 to 2020. Employing a Generalised Structural Equation Model (GSEM), the results confirm all three structural hypotheses: trade openness positively and significantly promotes financial development (H1a); financial development positively and significantly enhances tax revenue mobilisation (H1b); and financial development constitutes a significant indirect channel through which trade openness raises tax revenue (H1c). Results are robust to replacing domestic credit with the IMF composite Financial Development Index. The findings carry direct policy implications: trade liberalisation and financial sector development are complementary fiscal instruments in developing countries, and their joint pursuit, within a supportive institutional environment, is essential for sustainable domestic revenue mobilisation.

title: Progress of Circular Cities: Concept, Approach, and Examples
affiliations: University of Jaén

detail.title: Progress of Circular Cities: Concept, Approach, and Examples
detail.abstract: This paper reports a systematic review of the literature on circular cities, synthesizing 70 peer-reviewed and grey literature sources to examine conceptual foundations, methodological approaches, and empirical cases across European, Asian, and global contexts. Literature search across Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar (2018-2025) identified studies addressing circular economy transitions at the urban scale. Thematic analysis of these sources reveals a field evolving from waste-focused recycling initiatives toward integrated digital governance frameworks that combine artificial intelligence, blockchain, and urban metabolism assessment. Key findings include: (1) the convergence of digital technologies with circular governance creates unprecedented opportunities for transparent, scalable urban resource management; (2) monitoring and evaluation frameworks remain underdeveloped, constraining comparative assessment and evidence-based policy; (3) cultural and institutional context significantly mediates the effectiveness of circular city interventions; and (4) European and Japanese case studies demonstrate divergent but complementary pathways for implementation. The review identifies persistent gaps in longitudinal empirical research, standardized indicators, multi-level governance coordination, and Global South evidence. These findings inform recommendations for researchers, policymakers, and practitioners seeking to advance circular cities from experimental initiatives to mainstream urban development practice.

title: Venture Capital, Systemic Risk, and the Price of Downside Insurance: A Real Options Approach to the VIX
affiliations: , Sapienza University of Rome, Sapienza University of Rome and Sapienza University of Rome

detail.title: Venture Capital, Systemic Risk, and the Price of Downside Insurance: A Real Options Approach to the VIX
detail.abstract: This paper develops a unified theoretical framework linking venture capital financing, real option theory, and financial market volatility. Venture capital portfolios are modelled as systems of correlated real options on innovative projects, each driven by a geometric Brownian motion with shared macro-financial factor loadings. Positive cross-portfolio correlation generates non-linear aggregate variance that rises quadratically with portfolio size, giving rise to a systemic liability option, i.e., the expected aggregate loss imposed on the stakeholder network of portfolio companies when correlated option exercises occur. The liability option expected value is proportional to average correlation, aggregate variance, and the macroeconomic scale of the sector relative to GDP. In the proposed resilience framework, the net value of the venture capital system equals the aggregate asset option value minus this systemic liability, and a closed-form Systemic Resilience Index is derived. A dedicated section integrates the micro-level model of firm resilience and adaptive flexibility-including four critical indicators: the Resilience Index, the Adaptive Resilience Index, the liability parameter, and the net adaptive value of flexibility-and shows how these firm-level constructs aggregate into the macro-financial mechanisms through which venture capital affects the Volatility Index (VIX). The paper further corrects a widespread mischaracterization of the VIX: the VIX is not a measure of implied variance but a model-free price index of out-of-the-money, predominantly put options, that approximates the market's willingness to pay for downside insurance. Two main propositions formalize the structural link between real liability options and the VIX. A numerical simulation calibrated to a geopolitical shock illustrates the quantitative plausibility of the mechanism. An appendix proposes an empirical panel strategy to test the theoretical predictions.

title: Trustworthy AI for Wealth Management: Enhancing Investment Outcomes Through Interpretability, Forecasting, and Risk-Aware Optimisation
affiliations: University of Birmingham,  and Stratiphy Limited

detail.title: Trustworthy AI for Wealth Management: Enhancing Investment Outcomes Through Interpretability, Forecasting, and Risk-Aware Optimisation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Daniel Gold is founder and CEO of Stratiphy Limited.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) through Innovate UK grant number 10094067, Stratlib.AI: a trusted machine learning platform for asset and credit managers (PIs: Daniel Gold, Karen Elliott, and John Cartlidge).

detail.abstract: This paper presents a high-level synthesis of a UK Research and Innovation (UKRI)-funded research programme, translating recent advances in artificial intelligence into practical applications for wealth management and risk-aware investment decision-making. It addresses persistent investor challenges related to complexity, limited information, and lack of transparency. We make three contributions. First, we bring together a Cross-Modal Temporal Fusion (CMTF) model that integrates historical prices, macroeconomic indicators, financial news, and corporate reports to enhance forecasting accuracy, achieving a 30.38% improvement in recall relative to baseline models. Second, we incorporate a risk-aware portfolio optimisation approach based on adaptive weighted Lagrangian estimation, which balances return maximisation with variance minimisation while improving model stability and interpretability. Third, we examine how these methods align with emerging regulatory frameworks, including the Financial Conduct Authority's Targeted Support and Simplified Advice initiatives and broader Consumer Duty requirements. Empirical deployment on S&P500 stocks, with a medium risk appetite yields representative returns of 24.2%, which are much greater than the index 3.4% and iShares MSCI USA Momentum Factor ETF (MTUM) 3.6%. Stratiphy's portfolio achieved a Sharpe ratio of 1.84, versus 0.46 for the S&P500 and 0.33 for MTUM. The portfolio exhibited resilience to the significant global financial instability caused by US/Israel conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February, returns of 24.2% over a five-month period compared to 3.4% for the benchmark index, without a corresponding increase in volatility. These findings demonstrate how embedding interpretability, robustness, and regulatory alignment within AI systems can deliver more accessible, transparent, and effective wealth management solutions. The underlying technologies have been developed and validated in prior conference publications, here, we focus on their integration, practical deployment, and implications for financial services practice.

title: Automation and Disability: How Functional Limitations Shape Vulnerability to Technological Change
affiliations: Northwestern University and Northwestern University - School of Education and Social Policy

detail.title: Automation and Disability: How Functional Limitations Shape Vulnerability to Technological Change

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: Broad demographic categories used to identify populations at risk from technological change can aggregate workers with opposing exposures and obscure who is actually affected. We document this for disability and industrial robot adoption. Instrumenting U.S. robot exposure across 722 commuting zones with industry-level penetration in seven European economies, we find that robot adoption over 1993 to 2014 reduces employment by 3.4 percentage points for workers with disabilities and 3.7 for workers without, effects that are statistically indistinguishable. This aggregate similarity masks substantial heterogeneity by functional limitation. Workers with sensory impairments experience employment declines of 5.5 percentage points, roughly 50 percent above the aggregate, while workers with cognitive difficulties show no significant effect. Within-disability heterogeneity exceeds the betweengroup difference, suggesting that vulnerability to automation is determined by the interaction between specific functional limitations and the task content that robots displace, rather than by disability status per se.
